The math-minus-nonmath contrast grows smoothly over most of the depth, with one exception: layer 7. There it nearly doubles, from 0.26 to 0.46 of the residual norm on content tokens and from 0.18 to 0.39 at the last prompt token. At the last prompt token its direction also turns more than at any other layer (cosine 0.45 to the previous layer). Beyond layer 10 the contrast is stable (0.6–0.7) and turns little.

The large overall size is expected, since math word problems and poems or explanations differ in content. But the abrupt step at L7 marks the layer where most of the math-specific signal is written. Either L7's attention or its MLP writes it, and an implanted "math vector" would sit there.

The MLP part can be checked within the rules by applying L7's weights only to summary vectors. I take the mean activation difference (math minus nonmath prompts, content tokens, pass 6), map it through down_proj, and fold it through the post-feedforward norm scale. Then I compare that write with the measured jump in the contrast (L6→L7), and do the same for neighbouring layers 5–10. I also measure how concentrated the write is in its top neurons.
- If L7's MLP write aligns with the jump and a handful of neurons carry most of it, those neurons are a concrete candidate to ablate.
- If the write is diffuse, or the jump comes mostly from attention, I note that and move on.

The MLPs do not write the layer-7 jump. In layers 5–10 the MLP's math-minus-nonmath write is almost unrelated to the jump in the contrast (cosine −0.24 to +0.15). It is also diffuse: the top 5 neurons carry 3–15% of it and the top 50 only 13–23%. The jump at L7 is therefore attention gathering the problem's context into each token, ordinary context integration, and no planted math writer sits in these MLPs.

One cheap, coarse tampering route is left. A designer could rescale an entire layer's contribution through its norm scales, for example halving a post-attention or post-feedforward norm vector, which damps that layer without any odd structure inside the matrices. My earlier norm scan counted only zeros and near-zeros, not each layer's overall scale relative to its neighbours.

I will print, per layer, the median effective scale |1 + w| of the four layer norms and of the q/k norms. A layer whose scale breaks sharply from a smooth depth trend (for example 2–3× below both neighbours) would be a damping candidate to restore and test. A smooth profile closes the norm-scale line.

Ten of the eleven heads with a dominant write are ordinary sink heads. Their top output direction lies mostly along the massive dimensions and the mean residual (cosine 0.55–0.99). L11h3 and L11h2, the heads that broadcast the end of the prompt, are at 0.99 and 0.97: they maintain the massive activations, nothing more.

The exception is **L22h0**, a late local-layer head. Its dominant output direction is unrelated to the mean residual (0.05), the massive dimensions (0.07), D1 (0.02) and the math contrast (0.08). It also has the lowest effective output rank of all 104 heads (54, against a typical 150–200). It sits four layers before the output and writes a strong, non-bookkeeping direction, so its write could act directly on next-token choice.

I will see what its top three output directions do to the logits. Each direction goes through the final norm scale and the tied unembedding. I report z-scores for a fixed list of task-relevant tokens: digits, operators, "=", "####", "Let", "$", "**", newline, end-of-turn and EOS. I also count how many digit tokens are among the 200 most promoted and most suppressed, so no vocabulary list gets printed.

If a top direction strongly favours or suppresses digits, operators or the answer marker, L22h0 could steer numerical choices and becomes a concrete ablation candidate. If the effects on these tokens are unremarkable, it is a specialized but irrelevant head.
